outcome: The full Birkhoff conjecture (every strictly convex integrable billiard boundary is an ellipse) remains open, but two genuine cases were settled and published within the window: Illya Koval proved a local version (an integrable perturbation of almost every ellipse, preserving integrability near the boundary, must itself be an ellipse), published in Inventiones Mathematicae in December 2025; and Kaloshin, Koudjinan & Zhang proved that a domain close enough to a centrally-symmetric one with an integrable billiard is an ellipse, with a substantially revised version posted in September 2024.
summary: The triage correctly identified Koval's local Birkhoff conjecture result as the most decisive item, but its arXiv preprint (v1 Nov 2021, v2 Feb 2023) predates the frozen revision; what actually falls inside the window is the paper's appearance in Inventiones Mathematicae (published online 11 Dec 2025, vol. 244, pp. 221-298), which is when this result was digested/certified by a journal of record, so I treat it as the event that brought this case to `resolved-within-the-window` status for that restricted case, while keeping the record's overall `status` as `partial` because it only settles a case (integrable perturbations of almost every ellipse), not the full conjecture. A second, independently useful case restriction is Kaloshin-Koudjinan-Zhang's 'Birkhoff Conjecture for nearly centrally symmetric domains' (arXiv 2306.12301): a domain sufficiently close to a centrally-symmetric one with an integrable billiard must be an ellipse. Its original submission (21 June 2023) predates the window, but a heavily revised v2 (19 September 2024, described in the arXiv changelog as an improvement to 'content and presentation' with the file size roughly halved) falls inside it; I dated the decisive `event` to this revision since it is the first written argument in the form now citable, though the underlying claim may have existed earlier in substance. I checked several other 2024-2026 papers that surface when searching 'Birkhoff conjecture': Kepler billiards (Baranzini-Barutello-De Blasi-Terracini, arXiv 2507.08446, July 2025) proves an analogous statement for billiards in a gravitational (Kepler) potential -- a different dynamical setting, so it is a related problem, not a case, and does not change this bullet. The 'rationally/polynomially integrable planar dual and projective billiards' line of work (Glutsyuk et al., e.g. arXiv 2112.07056, 2301.00464, and the newer Inventiones paper 'On rationally integrable planar dual and projective billiards') concerns dual/projective billiards, a distinct notion of billiard dynamics (reflections of tangent lines to caustics rather than the standard inner-billiard reflection law), so these too are variants rather than cases of the stated conjecture. Koval's separate paper on Gevrey divergence of Birkhoff normal forms (arXiv 2403.14448, submitted March 2024) is about analytic regularity of normal forms near periodic orbits, a related but distinct question, not a case restriction of the ellipse conjecture. No source anywhere in this search -- the papers themselves, the Wikipedia article (which returned 404 on fetch and could not be checked directly, though its content is mirrored in search-engine summaries), or general web searches for AI/machine-learning involvement in Birkhoff-conjecture work -- turned up any AI system contributing to any of these proofs; all are traditional human mathematical arguments (dynamical systems, KAM-type perturbation theory, complex-analytic and wave-trace methods) with no computer-algebra or numerical-verification component either, aside from illustrative numerical simulations of chaotic Kepler-billiard trajectories in the Kepler paper, which play no role in that paper's proof.
competing_reading: One could argue the `event` date should instead be Koval's Inventiones online-publication date (2025-12-11) rather than the September 2024 arXiv revision of the Kaloshin-Koudjinan-Zhang paper, since Koval's is arguably the more decisive/cited case restriction and per §6.3 journal publication dates are normally to be avoided in favor of first written argument -- but Koval's first written argument (the arXiv preprint) predates the window entirely, so if that paper is to count as an in-window event at all it can only be via its journal appearance, which is unusual under the dating rule. An alternative, more conservative reading is that Koval's result should be treated as `open_stale` for dating purposes (its substantive mathematical content was already public by Feb 2023) and only the Kaloshin-Koudjinan-Zhang September 2024 revision counts as a genuine in-window case-restriction event, which is the reading I adopted for `event`, while still describing Koval's Inventiones publication in `outcome`/`summary` as a second, independently useful data point about the field's overall progress.
what_would_settle_it: Access to the Kaloshin-Koudjinan-Zhang v1-to-v2 diff (or the authors' own account) to confirm whether the September 2024 revision changed the mathematical result versus only exposition, which would determine whether that revision is truly the first written argument for a new claim or merely a rewrite of an already-public 2023 result; and a full read of Koval's Inventiones referee reports or acknowledgements (not accessible without a subscription) to confirm no computational or AI-assisted component was used, beyond what the freely-available arXiv preprint shows.

judgement.doubts: Both case results predate the snapshot by their first written arguments (Koval arXiv Nov 2021; KKZ arXiv 21 June 2023). Koval's Dec 2025 Inventiones publication and KKZ's Sept 2024 v2 ('content and presentation') are not new events. The record's `event` field still points to the KKZ v2 revision; it no longer sets the status. Kepler billiards and dual/projective billiards papers are variants.
